newsitem.title: USA: Gore, Powell head Reuters poll for presidency.
newsitem.headline: Gore, Powell head Reuters poll for presidency.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent

Vice President Al Gore starts his quest for Democratic presidential nomination in 2000 as the frontrunner, while retired Gen. Colin Powell and Texas Gov. George Bush lead the Republican field, according to a Reuters poll released on Sunday.

In the poll of 1,008 registered voters, conducted for Reuters by John Zogby International on Jan. 25-29, 53 percent of Democrats in the survey said Gore was their choice for the next president of the United States.

Almost 10 percent preferred former New Jersey Sen. Bill Bradley, 9 percent liked House of Representatives Minority Leader Richard Gephardt and 5 percent said they would support Nebraska Sen. Bob Kerrey.

Among Republicans, Powell led with 29 percent. Bush, the eldest son of former President George Bush, was second with 15 percent. Defeated vice presidential candidate Jack Kemp had 12 percent, former Vice President Dan Quayle had 11 percent, Tennessee Sen. Fred Thompson came in with 6 percent, former Education Secretary Lamar Alexander and New Jersey Gov. Christine Tood Whitman, each harvested 4 percent.
Although the presidential race will not get underway in earnest for another two years, politicians in both parties are already jockeying for position.
The poll margin of error overall was plus or minus 3.2 percentage points. It should be noted that the margin of error may be substantially larger for sub groups within the survey.
On the Republican side, Kemp is about to launch a political action committee while Bush and Alexander have openly expressed some interest in running.
Thompson has the chance to take the public spotlight as chairman of the Senate committee that will investigate alleged wrongdoing by Democratic Party fundraisers.
Powell, who decided not to take part in the 1996 presidential race, is considered by many Republicans as too moderate to win the party's presidential nomination.
In one-on-one matchups between candidates, Powell was the only one to beat Gore, by 49 percent to 35 percent. But Gore beat all the other Republicans.

He beat Kemp by 53 percent to 34 percent, Quayle by 58 percent to 27 percent and Bush by 47 percent to 39 percent. One of the surprises in the poll was the relative strength of the younger Bush, whose name is recognised by many because of his father.

Others in the poll may find it hard to win name recognition. For example Alexander, who put up a credible campaign for the Republican nomination in 1996, was still unknown to 42 percent in the survey and had only a 26 percent favourability rating.
Gephardt was viewed favourably by 25 percent, with 53 percent saying they were not familar with him. In contrast, Gore had 67 percent favourability, while 26 percent viewed him unfavourably.
